questions.stem: Consider the sentence: "The old lighthouse stood silently above the cliffs." Identify (a) the adjective and (b) the adverb.
markscheme: B1: the adjective is "old" (it describes the noun "lighthouse")
B1: the adverb is "silently" (it describes how the lighthouse stood)
questions.modelAnswer: The adjective is "old": it describes the noun "lighthouse". The adverb is "silently": it describes the verb "stood", telling us how the lighthouse stood. (Note that "above" is a preposition here, not an adverb.)

questions.stem: Identify the language technique used in this sentence, and quote the words that show it: "The classroom was a zoo by the time the supply teacher arrived."
markscheme: B1: identifies the technique as a metaphor
B1: quotes "the classroom was a zoo" (direct comparison without "like" or "as")
questions.modelAnswer: The technique is a metaphor. The classroom is said to BE "a zoo" — a direct comparison without "like" or "as" — suggesting chaos, noise and wild behaviour. (If it used "like" or "as" it would be a simile instead.)

questions.stem: Read Passage A: "The lights went out. At first nobody moved. Then, one by one, the windows of Rowan Street flickered with candle flames, like small orange eyes opening in the dark. Sam pressed his nose to the cold glass and watched the street below. His mother moved through the kitchen with a torch, steady as anything, its beam swinging across cups and plates. The radio murmured somewhere behind her, low and crackling. "Storm's knocked the lines down," she said. "Could be hours." Sam pulled his coat tighter, although he was indoors. Down the street, a dog began to bark, and somebody answered with a laugh. The fear in Sam's chest loosened, little by little. By the time the first snowflake touched the window, he had decided the blackout might not be a disaster after all. It might, he thought, be an adventure." What is Sam's mother carrying, and what does she say caused the blackout?
markscheme: B1: she is carrying a torch
B1: the storm has knocked the power lines down
questions.modelAnswer: Sam's mother is carrying a torch ("moved through the kitchen with a torch"). She says the storm caused the blackout: "Storm's knocked the lines down," and adds that it "Could be hours" before the power returns.

questions.stem: Look again at Passage A (Question 3). What can you infer about Sam's mother? Make one clear inference and support it with TWO different quotations from the passage.
markscheme: B1: valid inference, e.g. she is calm / composed / practical / unfazed by the blackout
B1: first supporting quotation, e.g. "steady as anything"
B1: second, different quotation, e.g. "moved through the kitchen with a torch" or "Could be hours"
questions.modelAnswer: Sam's mother seems calm and practical, as if the blackout is no crisis. The writer says she moved "steady as anything", which shows she is completely composed, and she simply gets on with things, moving "through the kitchen with a torch". Her matter-of-fact remark "Could be hours" also suggests she is unfazed and already planning around the problem.

questions.stem: Identify ONE language technique in this line from Passage A and explain its effect on the reader: "the windows of Rowan Street flickered with candle flames, like small orange eyes opening in the dark." [3 marks]
markscheme: B1: identifies a technique — simile ("like small orange eyes") or personification (the street given eyes)
B1: explains the effect — the houses seem alive, waking up and watching; warm but slightly eerie
B1: links to the reader — draws us into a quiet, watchful atmosphere, making the blackout feel strange and almost magical
questions.modelAnswer: The line uses a simile: the candle flames are compared to "small orange eyes opening in the dark". This makes the houses of Rowan Street seem alive, as if they are waking up one by one and watching — a warm image (orange, candlelight) with a slightly eerie edge (eyes in the dark). The reader is drawn into a hushed, watchful atmosphere in which the blackout feels strange and almost magical rather than simply frightening. Personification is also acceptable, since the street is given eyes.

questions.stem: A speaker campaigning to save a local market asks: "Do we want a town centre full of shuttered shops?" State the answer the speaker wants from the audience, and explain why asking a question works better here than making a statement.
markscheme: B1: the speaker wants the audience to answer "no" and picture the decline of their town centre
B1: a rhetorical question pulls the audience in — they reach the conclusion themselves, which is more persuasive than being told it
questions.modelAnswer: The speaker wants the audience to answer "no" in their heads and to picture their town centre decaying, full of closed shops. Asking a rhetorical question works better than a statement like "We do not want shuttered shops" because it pulls listeners in and makes them reach the speaker's conclusion for themselves — an idea people arrive at on their own feels more convincing than one they are simply told.

questions.stem: Passage A opens with the four-word sentence "The lights went out." Explain TWO effects of opening the passage with such a short sentence.
markscheme: B1: the sudden, blunt sentence imitates the blackout itself — abrupt and shocking
B1: it hooks the reader at once, raising questions (why? what happens next?)
B1: it establishes the central event/problem of the whole passage immediately
questions.modelAnswer: First, the short, blunt sentence imitates the event itself: the blackout happens suddenly, and the writing cuts off just as abruptly, so the reader feels the shock. Second, it hooks the reader immediately — four words raise questions (Why did the lights go out? What happens now?) that make us want to read on. It also establishes the central problem of the whole passage in the very first line: everything that follows grows out of the blackout.

questions.stem: Look at Passage A as a whole. How do Sam's feelings change between the start and the end of the passage? Support your answer with ONE quotation from the beginning and ONE from the end.
markscheme: B1: identifies the change — fear/nervousness at the start gives way to excitement/positivity by the end
B1: early quotation, e.g. "Sam pulled his coat tighter, although he was indoors" or "The fear in Sam's chest"
B1: closing quotation, e.g. "It might, he thought, be an adventure." or "the blackout might not be a disaster after all"
questions.modelAnswer: Sam starts frightened and ends excited. Early on, his fear is physical: he "pulled his coat tighter, although he was indoors", and the writer refers directly to "The fear in Sam's chest". Gradually, though, the street's sounds (the dog, the laugh) reassure him: "The fear in Sam's chest loosened, little by little". By the end he has reframed the whole event, deciding the blackout "might not be a disaster after all" and that "It might, he thought, be an adventure." His feelings have shifted from fear to hopeful excitement.
